Neonatal individuals of Bradypus tridactylus emerge at a surprisingly modest mass, with newborns weighing approximately 179 grams [Wwb = approximately 179 grams]. This relatively low birth weight, typical of arboreal folivores, is followed by a period of intensive maternal care during which the offspring remains tightly clutched to the mother’s ventrum. The weaning process is notably protracted for a mammal of this body size; field records indicate that nutritional independence is achieved roughly 4 months after parturition, corresponding to a weaning age of 122 days [tx = 122 days] when calculated under stable ambient conditions averaging 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. At the point of weaning, the young sloth attains a wet weight of 300 grams [Wwx = 300 grams], representing a substantial increase from its birth mass but still less than a tenth of the adult size. This extended period of lactational dependency is energetically costly for the mother, who must sustain her own slow metabolism while provisioning a growing offspring, a life-history strategy that is characteristic of the genus Bradypus.

Gestation in the pale-throated sloth spans 141 days [tg = 141 days] when females are maintained at a mean core temperature of approximately 33 °C [T = 33 °C], reflecting the species' remarkably low basal metabolic rate. This gestational period is relatively long for a eutherian mammal of this size, a pattern linked to the sloth's reduced metabolic capacity and its reliance on a low-energy folivorous diet. The single offspring is born fully furred and with its eyes open, a precocial condition that nonetheless requires several months of close association with the mother. Following parturition, the female enters a period of lactational amenorrhea, during which no further ovulations occur. Available data indicate that the maximum reproductive rate under these thermal conditions is one offspring every 616 days [Ri = one offspring every 616 days], a remarkably slow pace even among xenarthrans. This interbirth interval is among the longest recorded for any placental mammal of comparable body mass, underscoring the extreme energy limitations under which these animals operate. The combination of a modest birth weight, an extended gestation, and an exceptionally prolonged period between successive births defines a life-history strategy that is highly specialized for a low-metabolism, low-energy niche.

Sexual maturation in females is a notably slow process, with puberty occurring at 1642 days after birth [tp = 1642 days after birth] under the thermal conditions typical of the species' preferred microhabitat, which averages 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This extraordinarily late onset of reproductive maturity, equivalent to roughly 4.5 years, is among the latest recorded for any mammal of this size and reflects the protracted somatic development necessitated by their extremely low basal metabolic expenditure. Males, by contrast, achieve reproductive maturity somewhat earlier, reaching puberty at 1095 days after birth [tp = 1095 days after birth] under identical thermal conditions at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This sex difference in the pace of maturation, with females lagging behind males by over a year, may arise from the greater energetic demands that gestation and lactation impose on female body condition, requiring a longer period of somatic growth to accumulate sufficient reserves. The delayed female maturity is a critical constraint on population growth in this species, contributing to its characteristically slow life-history pace even by the standards of neotropical arboreal mammals.

The maximum longevity of Bradypus tridactylus has been documented at just over 31 years [am = 31 years] under captive conditions when individuals are maintained at a thermal regime near 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a lifespan that is exceptional for a mammal of its mass and metabolic rate. This extended survival is consistent with the broader life-history syndrome observed in xenarthrans, which typically exhibit reduced senescence rates and prolonged reproductive windows. For context, the maximum adult body mass attained by females reaches approximately 4850 grams [Wwi = approximately 4850 grams], although individuals can range from 3.8 to 6.5 kilograms; males are consistently smaller, with an ultimate wet weight of 4600 grams [Wwi = 4600 grams] and a typical range of 3.2 to 6 kilograms. This modest degree of sexual size dimorphism, with females being slightly heavier, is typical of arboreal folivores where male-male competition is less pronounced than in terrestrial mammals. The attainment of these adult masses requires several years of sustained growth, a trajectory heavily influenced by the quality and availability of young leaves in the canopy.

Respirometry trials conducted under controlled laboratory conditions have established that the resting metabolic rate of Bradypus tridactylus is remarkably low, with a maximal basal oxygen consumption of 580.6 milliliters per hour [JOi = 580.6 milliliters per hour] when measured at a thermoneutral ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This value is among the lowest mass-specific metabolic rates ever recorded for a placental mammal, reflecting the sloth's extreme adaptations for energy conservation. The relationship between energy intake and reproductive output is particularly tight in this species; the observed maximum reproductive rate of one offspring per 616 days [Ri = one offspring per 616 days] is directly constrained by the limited metabolic power available for gestation and lactation. The long lifespan, extremely late female maturity, and exceptionally low reproductive output together paint a portrait of a species whose entire life-history is calibrated around minimizing energy expenditure in an environment where high-quality food resources are both scarce and difficult to digest.
